KEY MESSAGE 1...Daily chances for showers and thunderstorms 
will return today and into the middle of the week. There is a 
risk for strong to severe thunderstorms, as well as a marginal 
risk for localized heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding.

A mid-level shortwave trough will approach the area this 
afternoon into the evening as mean flow shifts more westerly and
mid- level flow increases amid falling heights. Model consensus
suggest this will arrive right around peak diurnal instability
in the mid to late afternoon hours. Convection is already
ongoing with this feature across western Pennsylvania and into
the Ohio River Valley, which could either maintain itself into 
our region by afternoon, or weaken and restrengthen. As it 
typically the case with these setups, the CAMs are varying 
significantly in their solutions, but the synoptic evolution 
supports an outcome as previously described.

SPC has expanded the Slight Risk (level 2 out of 5) Risk for 
severe thunderstorms farther east to include almost our entire
region, save for a small portion of southeastern Delaware. 
There remains some uncertainty in exactly how convection will 
evolve this afternoon, and thus which areas will be at greater 
risk for severe storms, so we'll have to monitor trends upstream
closely as the day progresses.

The primary risk with any thunderstorms today will be damaging 
wind gusts, as there looks to be more of an upscale growth 
potential into a line segment(s) as the activity approaches our
area. Instability of 2000-3000 J/kg and low-level lapse rates
upward of 8C/km are supportive of damaging wind gusts, and deep
layer shear in the 25-35 kt range will support organized
convection. The line of storms will likely be fairly fast
moving, say 40-50 mph, so this should be a quick hitting event. 
The tornado threat, while still non-zero, will be very limited
as LCLs will be fairly high and low level shear is meager at
best. As for flash flooding, there is a Marginal (level 1 out 
4) Risk for excessive rainfall for our entire area. PWATs do 
look to increase again to upwards of 2 inches, so there is heavy
rain potential. However, with a quick moving linear storm mode 
anticipated, this will limit the potential for flash flooding. 

There remains some uncertainty around the exact timing of the 
convection today, though with that said, the most favorable 
timing is focusing in on the mid afternoon to early evening 
hours, generally between 3 PM and 9 PM.

The trend for lower instability has continued for Tuesday given
the faster evolution of the synoptic features (cold front and 
shortwave trough). Tuesday's activity will be displaced to our 
southwest. With that said, we could still see some convection 
potential, or even get the remnants of whatever occurs upstream
later in the evening. So while the threat of severe storms now 
appears to be lower for Tuesday, we could still get showers and
storms in some form. Details for Tuesday are even more 
uncertain than Monday, and Monday's activity will probably play 
some role in what exactly happens Tuesday. SPC expanded the
Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 5) farther northeast into the
Philly metro area, and the entire area remains in the Marginal
Risk (level 1 out of 4) for excessive rainfall.

A cold front looks to stall to our northwest Tuesday into 
Wednesday. Multiple waves look to ride along the stalled 
boundary which will support diurnally driven convection 
continuing at least through Wednesday, and possible Thursday. 
The front looks to push through by late Thursday, and a much 
drier and cooler airmass will arrive by Friday and Saturday as a
result. This will bring us a more pronounced break in 
convective potential and more pleasant weather conditions.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Hot and humid conditions will persist into the 
middle of the week, but humidity will not be as oppressive as 
recent days.

A relatively stagnant synoptic pattern will remain in place 
across our region. Quasi zonal mid and upper level flow will be 
in place through the middle of the week as Bermuda high pressure
persists offshore. This will keep a very warm and moist airmass
in place across the region through the period.

Hot and humid conditions will continue into the middle of the
week, although slightly lower temperatures and dewpoints will
arrive for Wednesday. Dewpoints are anticipated to mix out into
the mid to upper 60s again this afternoon. This will give some 
slight reprieve from the excessive humidity we've experienced in
recent days, though highs will still be in the upper 80s to mid
90s. The lower dewpoints will result in maximum heat indices 
mainly in the mid to upper 90s, though could get near 100 
degrees in Delmarva and near the coast in New Jersey. Since the 
forecast is decidedly below criteria, we have opted to continue 
without a new Heat Advisory, though it will still be hot and 
humid.
